paragraphs.text: The leaf comes from [Da Xue Shan](da-xue-shan:where-it-is), Big Snow Mountain, a name Yunnan gives to more than one mountain; Lincang alone has four. When the trade uses the name on its own it most often means the [Mengku peak](da-xue-shan:which-one), the main summit of the Bangma ridge on the border of Shuangjiang and Gengma counties, but the name by itself does not settle which mountain a tea is from. [Wild tree tea](da-xue-shan:wild-and-old), ancient garden tea and plantation tea are three different things, and all three are sold under this name.

This is a cake of [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from 2005. After the wok, raw pu’er is [dried in the sun](sheng:making) and never with hot air, so some of the leaf’s own activity survives, and that is what lets it keep changing for years. At twenty-one years it is past both points the trade gives for when [aged](sheng:ageing) begins: ten years for some, twenty or more for many. How far it has come depends on its [storage](sheng:storage), because the change is partly slow oxidation and partly the work of microbes, so heat and humidity set the pace.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
